title: The Coppersmith's Son: Gaudí, the Patron, and the Temple He Left One Fifth Built
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Reus and the Camp de Tarragona

stops.name: Reus, the coppersmith's fifth child
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a manufacturing town of aguardiente and cotton, second in Catalonia only to Barcelona, the coppersmith Francesc Gaudí i Serra and his wife Antònia Cornet i Bertran have their fifth and last child. Both families are coppersmiths, generations of them. The trade is the beating of a flat sheet over a form until it holds a volume, and the workshop where it is done sits under the rooms where the boy will grow up. They name him Antoni. Of the five children born into that house, three will not outlive their parents.
suggested_refs: The Gaudí family's coppersmith workshop at Reus, and the boiler trade of the Camp de Tarragona
sources: Reus civil and parish records, cited in Bergós and Van Hensbergen

stops.name: Església Prioral de Sant Pere, the baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: One day old, he is carried to the priory church at the centre of Reus and baptized Antoni Plàcid Guillem Gaudí i Cornet. This register is the whole documentary case for Reus as his birthplace, and the neighbouring village of Riudoms has been disputing it ever since. The infant is already sick and stays sick. Rheumatic complaints keep him out of school for long stretches and away from the games of the other children, and when the family walks out to the farm he goes on a donkey.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Sant Pere de Reus, the single document naming Reus as his birthplace

stops.name: Riudoms, the farmhouse the village still claims
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the birthplace is disputed and unresolved. Two lenses of this research placed the Mas de la Calderera differently (41.1631, 1.0739 against a chronology value 5.9 km off), so the checkable village coordinate is pinned rather than the farmhouse
stops.campa: Six kilometres from Reus his mother's people work the land from a farmhouse called the Mas de la Calderera. The boy is sent here through the long stretches when he is too ill for school, and Riudoms has claimed for a century that he was not merely raised here but born here. The register in Reus says otherwise and nothing reconciles the two. What the countryside gives him is not in dispute. He spends those months out of doors and close to the ground, under the vault a fig tree makes over a boy who cannot run, near enough to a snail shell to learn how it is wound.
stops.quote: Originality is returning to the origin.
stops.quote_source: Antoni Gaudí, recorded by his disciples; Isidre Puig Boada, El pensament de Gaudí (Barcelona: Col·legi d'Arquitectes de Catalunya, 1981), p. 13
suggested_refs: The Mas de la Calderera at Riudoms, and the century-old Reus/Riudoms dispute over the birth
sources: Riudoms local tradition, contested against the Reus baptismal record

stops.name: Escoles Pies de Reus, the handwritten magazine
stops.date_confidence: attested; he is at the school 1863-1868
stops.campa: At eleven he enters the Piarist fathers' school. His marks are unremarkable. With two friends, Eduard Toda and Josep Ribera, he makes a handwritten magazine called El Arlequín and fills it with drawings, and the three of them draw up a scheme for restoring the ruined Cistercian monastery of Poblet, a project on a scale no schoolboy could execute and which none of them gives up quickly. He is a boy who cannot easily explain himself in words and can already draw almost anything put in front of him. The drawings for El Arlequín and for Poblet are the earliest surviving evidence of his hand.
suggested_refs: El Arlequín, the schoolboy magazine of Gaudí, Toda and Ribera
The boys' restoration scheme for the monastery of Poblet
sources: School records and Toda/Ribera recollections, cited in the Bergós biography

stops.name: La Llotja, the draughtsman paying his own way
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Llotja years run c.1868/1870 to 1873
stops.campa: At sixteen he moves to Barcelona with his brother Francesc, who is reading medicine, and enrols at the school of design beside the old sea exchange on the harbour front. There is no money. He draws for practising architects to pay for his own courses and takes his preparatory sciences in whatever order the schools will grant them; five years pass before the architecture school proper will have him. The city he has come to is pulling down its medieval walls and laying the grid of the Eixample across the plain outside them.
suggested_refs: The Llotja de Mar school of design on the Passeig d'Isabel II

stops.name: Escola Tècnica Superior d'Arquitectura, the uneven student
stops.date_confidence: attested; 1873-1878. A chronology source in this research gave the span as 1876-1878, which covers only his final two years
stops.campa: Five years in the new higher school of architecture, and the record is lopsided: strong at drawing and at structural calculation, indifferent to the coursework he does not respect, failing subjects and sitting them again. Through these years he keeps a notebook, later called the Manuscrito de Reus, setting down what he thinks about ornament, the house, and the Christian temple. It is the only sustained text in his own hand that will survive him. Everything else that circulates as his doctrine was written down by other men who were listening when he spoke.
suggested_refs: The Manuscrito de Reus (1873-1878), the only substantial text in Gaudí's hand
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoni_Gaudí (on the disciple-compilers Ràfols, Bergós, Martinell, Puig i Boada)

stops.name: Reus, the year that halves the family
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: His mother Antònia dies at fifty-seven. His brother Francesc, qualified as a physician and not yet practising, dies at twenty-five. Gaudí is twenty-four and still a student, and from this year what remains of the household attaches itself to him: his father first, later an orphaned niece, following him from lodging to lodging for the rest of their lives. He is serving his military term through these same years as a Military Administrator, a desk posting that keeps him out of the Carlist fighting in the north.
suggested_refs: The deaths of Antònia Cornet and Francesc Gaudí the younger, Reus, 1876

stops.name: Parc de la Ciutadella, the water above the fountain
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Cascada is built 1875-1881, and his documented share is the reservoir calculation and the rockwork, not the ironwork sometimes credited to him
stops.campa: The old citadel has been pulled down and a park laid over its ground, and the architect Josep Fontserè is raising a monumental cascade at the edge of it. Gaudí, still a student, works on the project for wages. His documented contribution is the hydraulic calculation of the elevated reservoir that feeds the fountain, and the rockwork beneath it: how much water, how high, how held. It is the first structure standing in Barcelona that his arithmetic keeps up. The name on the work is Fontserè's.
suggested_refs: The Cascada of the Parc de la Ciutadella and its elevated water reservoir
sources: Fontserè project records, cited in the Van Hensbergen biography

stops.name: Barcelona, the degree and Rogent's sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year only; the day 15 March given by one source is unsupported, and the director's remark is an undocumented anecdote repeated across the biographies
stops.campa: The school hands him the title. Its director Elies Rogent is said to have remarked that they had given it either to a fool or to a genius and that time would show which; no archive holds the sentence and every biography prints it. What the archive holds is a new architect with a stamp, debts, and an appetite for gloves, gaiters, tailored suits and the opera, none of which will survive his forties. He is twenty-five. He begins signing his own drawings that spring.
suggested_refs: The 1878 degree roll of the Escola Tècnica Superior d'Arquitectura de Barcelona
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoni_Gaudí (year attested; quotation widely repeated, unsourced)

segments.name: First Commissions, and a Glass Case in Paris

stops.name: Plaça Reial, the lampposts
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The city commissions street lighting for the arcaded square off the Rambla, and the new architect designs cast-iron lampposts with six arms apiece, crowned with the winged helmet of Mercury, standing on a base of stone. He is twenty-six and has held his title for a matter of months. It is public work, paid and visible, and the first thing of his that the people of Barcelona walk past without any idea whose it is. The lamps are still in the square.
suggested_refs: The Gaudí lampposts of the Plaça Reial, Barcelona, 1878

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the vitrine that finds a patron
stops.date_confidence: attested for the display case and for the meeting it caused; the accounts hold that Gaudí did not travel to Paris and that the case was exhibited without him, so this pin marks his object rather than his presence
stops.campa: A glass and wrought-iron display case built for the glove maker Comella stands in the Spanish section of the Universal Exposition. Eusebi Güell, industrialist, heir to a textile fortune, stops in front of it and asks who made the thing. The answer begins a patronage of forty years, a dozen buildings, and a friendship that outlasts the money it was founded on. Whether Gaudí ever crossed the border to stand beside his own case is unsettled; the accounts that survive have it going to Paris on its own, with him at his board in Barcelona.
suggested_refs: The Comella glove-maker's vitrine, Paris Universal Exposition of 1878
sources: Van Hensbergen, Gaudí (on the Güell meeting and the case travelling alone)

stops.name: Mataró, the cooperative and the parabolic arch
stops.date_confidence: attested; the commission runs 1878-1882 and most of the scheme is never built
stops.campa: A workers' cooperative in the textile town up the coast hires him to plan a factory, housing for the members, and an assembly hall. He designs a bleaching shed carried on wooden parabolic arches, bolted, light and cheap, and a banner for the cooperative with the workers' motto on it. He will go on using that curve for the rest of his working life, and it will end up over the nave of the Sagrada Família. Almost none of the larger scheme at Mataró goes up; there is no money and the town has little patience.
suggested_refs: The Cooperativa Obrera Mataronense and its parabolic-arch bleaching shed
sources: Cooperativa Obrera Mataronense project archives, cited in standard biographies

stops.name: Mataró, Josefa Moreu
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the attraction is repeated across the biographies with no surviving correspondence, and the marriage proposal is the embellishment. One lens of this research wrongly placed her in Reus
stops.campa: Among the people running the cooperative is a teacher, Josefa Moreu, at work in the same rooms he is drawing in. The biographies agree that he was drawn to her and that she did not return it, and go on, without a document between them, to have him propose and be refused. After this year there is no woman in the record at all: no engagement, no household of his own, only his father, his niece, the work, and the church. Nothing in his own hand records any of it.
suggested_refs: Josefa Moreu, maestra of the Cooperativa Mataronense, c.1884

stops.name: Casa Vicens, the palm and the tile
stops.date_confidence: attested; plans signed 15 January 1883, presented to the Gràcia town council on 20 January, approved 1 March, built 1883-1885
stops.campa: For Manel Vicens i Montaner, a currency and stock broker whom half the literature still misdescribes as a tile manufacturer, he builds a summer house in what is then the separate town of Gràcia. Brick, rubble and green and white tile in checkerboard, Mudéjar and Orientalist motifs stacked up the corners, a smoking room ceiling of hanging plaster stalactites. A wild palm grew on the site before the digging. Llorenç Matamala moulds its fronds and Joan Oñós casts them in iron, so that the garden gate is made of the plant the house displaced.
suggested_refs: The palmetto gate of Casa Vicens, cast from a palm growing on the site
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_Vicens (client corrected to stock and currency broker)

stops.name: Sagrada Família, the crypt he inherits
stops.date_confidence: attested; he takes over in November 1883 and is formally appointed Architect Director on 28 March 1884
stops.campa: Francisco de Paula del Villar has laid the foundations of a crypt for an expiatory temple funded by alms, and resigns over a dispute about materials. The commission passes to Gaudí, thirty-one years old. He is formally appointed Architect Director the following March, and he throws out Villar's neo-Gothic scheme entire, keeping only what is already in the ground. He will work on this building for forty-three years. At his death it will stand somewhere between a sixth and a quarter finished.
stops.quote: My client is not in a hurry.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Gaudí; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagrada_Família gives it as 'Gaudí is said to have remarked'
suggested_refs: Villar's crypt foundations, the one part of the temple Gaudí did not design

stops.name: Comillas, the sunflower tower
stops.date_confidence: attested; built 1883-1885
stops.campa: On the Cantabrian coast, eight hundred kilometres from Barcelona, he builds a summer villa for Máximo Díaz de Quijano, a relative by marriage of the Marqués de Comillas. He works largely by correspondence and by drawings sent north. Bands of glazed sunflower tile wind around the tower in courses set so that they read as a sundial across the garden below. The client, who commissioned a house for a long retirement, dies within a year of its completion and hardly lives in it.
suggested_refs: El Capricho at Comillas and its sunflower-tile sundial

stops.name: Finca Güell, the dragon at the gate
stops.date_confidence: attested; pavilions and gate built 1884-1887. Coordinates corrected here by roughly 400 m from the value carried in this research pool
stops.campa: For the Güell estate at Pedralbes he rebuilds the gatehouse, the stables and the riding school, and forges a gate of wrought iron in the shape of a dragon with its jaw open and one claw raised. Above it stands an orange tree worked in antimony. The dragon is Ladon, guardian of the garden of the Hesperides in Jacint Verdaguer's L'Atlàntida, and the coils of its body are laid out to the star positions of the constellation Serpens. The gate is hinged so that opening it lifts the beast's foreleg at whoever is arriving.
suggested_refs: Jacint Verdaguer, L'Atlàntida, the source of the Hesperides programme at the Güell pavilions
sources: Güell estate records, cited in standard biographies

stops.name: Palau Güell, the perforated dome
stops.date_confidence: attested; built 1886-1888, not 1886-1890 as one lens of this research gave it
stops.campa: Güell wants a town house on a narrow street off the Rambla, in a quarter of brothels and cheap theatres, and gets one faced in grey Garraf stone with two parabolic arches for doors, wide enough to take a carriage and its horses down into basement stables. The central hall rises the full height of the building into a dome pierced with small round openings; at night lanterns are hung outside them and the room fills with what looks like a sky. Twenty chimneys stand on the roof, each dressed differently in broken tile.
stops.quote: Architecture's significance is shown when there dominates evidence of lofty intentions that triumph over all the problems in the line of fire (structure, economy, technique, utility). Thanks to interior preparation, architecture is the fruit of character, just that, a manifestation of character.
suggested_refs: The perforated central dome of Palau Güell, lit by lanterns hung from outside
sources: Palau Güell building records; UNESCO nomination file

stops.name: Barcelona waterfront, the Transatlántica pavilion
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Barcelona holds its own Universal Exposition on the ground of the demolished citadel and along the harbour, and the Compañía Transatlántica shipping line commissions a pavilion from him. He builds it in the Mudéjar idiom, arcaded and light, temporary by definition: it is the only thing he ever makes knowing the date of its demolition in advance. It comes down with the rest of the fair, and drawings and photographs are all that is left of it. Several other works of his first decade survive in the same way, on paper.
suggested_refs: The Compañía Transatlántica pavilion, Barcelona Universal Exposition of 1888, demolished

stops.name: Col·legi de les Teresianes, the corridor of arches
stops.date_confidence: attested; built 1888-1890. Coordinates corrected here by roughly 1.1 km from the value carried in this research pool
stops.campa: He takes over a half-built convent school from Joan Baptista Pons i Trabal, whose Byzantine scheme had got no further than foundations, and works under the Teresian rule of poverty: brick, no stone facing, no ornament he cannot justify to a treasurer. The top-floor corridor is a file of parabolic brick arches, whitewashed, each framing the next, running the length of the building toward a single window. Visitors have compared walking it to walking inside a rosary.
suggested_refs: The parabolic upper corridor of the Col·legi de les Teresianes, Carrer de Ganduxer

stops.name: Astorga, the palace and the bishop who dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; design approved February 1889, Grau dies in 1893 and Gaudí resigns the same year
stops.campa: Fire has taken the bishop's palace at Astorga, and the bishop, Joan Baptista Grau i Vallespinós, is a Catalan from the Camp de Tarragona who wants a Catalan architect. Gaudí sends drawings from Barcelona and fights the diocesan building committee over each of them. Grau dies in 1893. Without his patron Gaudí resigns the commission that same year and never goes back; the palace stands roofless for over a decade and is finished by Ricardo García Guereta between 1907 and 1915.
suggested_refs: The diocesan archive of Astorga, on the disputes over the palace design
sources: Diocesan archive of Astorga, cited in standard biographies

stops.name: León, Casa Botines
stops.date_confidence: attested; built 1891-1892
stops.campa: Two merchants of León, Simón Fernández and Mariano Andrés, want a warehouse for their textile business with apartments above it, on a square facing the Renaissance palace of the Guzmanes. He gives them a block of grey limestone with corner turrets and a dry moat letting light into the basement. Over the principal door, in the original design and carved by Llorenç Matamala i Piñol, Saint George puts his lance through the dragon. The building goes up in ten months.
suggested_refs: The Saint George of Casa Botines, carved by Llorenç Matamala i Piñol for the principal entrance

stops.name: Tangier, the mission that is never built
stops.date_confidence: attested for the journey and the design; the commission is never executed
stops.campa: The Marqués de Comillas is funding a Franciscan mission for Africa and sends Gaudí across the strait to look at ground. He goes by way of Málaga and comes back from Tangier with a design for a complex of parabolic towers, tapered and leaning inward, ringing a courtyard. No money follows the drawings and nothing is built. The tower form worked out here for a mission in Morocco that never exists will reappear, two decades later, over the nave of the Sagrada Família.
suggested_refs: Gaudí's unbuilt design for the Franciscan Catholic missions at Tangier, 1892-1893

stops.name: Garraf, the cellar on the cliff
stops.date_confidence: attested; built 1895-1897 under the site direction of Francesc Berenguer. Coordinates corrected here by roughly 14 km, the largest error in this research pool
stops.campa: On the Güell family's coastal estate south of Barcelona, between the limestone and the sea, a wine cellar goes up under a roof of stone slabs pitched so steeply that roof and wall become one surface, the whole thing standing on splayed legs like an animal set down on its haunches. The work on site is directed by Francesc Berenguer, his assistant, who holds no architect's title and builds much of Gaudí's work for him. Which of the two men drew this roof is not recorded anywhere, and the attribution has been argued over since.
suggested_refs: The Celler Güell at Garraf and the attribution question between Gaudí and Francesc Berenguer

stops.name: Casa Calvet, the only prize
stops.date_confidence: attested; built 1898-1900, prize awarded 1900. The client is contested: en.wikipedia names Andreu Calvet, other sources the heirs of Pere Màrtir Calvet
stops.campa: For a family of textile manufacturers he builds an apartment and business block on Carrer de Casp with the most conventional face of his career: Baroque, symmetrical, dressed Montjuïc stone, a facade that offends nobody on the street. The city council gives it the prize for the best building of 1900, the only official honour of his lifetime. Behind the front the restraint stops. The door handles are cast in the shape of a hand closing, and the stair rails already curl the way the later work will.
suggested_refs: The Barcelona city council building prize of 1900, awarded to Casa Calvet

stops.name: Colònia Güell, the hanging model
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1898 commission; construction runs 1908-1914 and is halted by the Güell family in 1914, not by Eusebi Güell's death, which comes in 1918. Coordinates corrected here by roughly 1 km
stops.campa: For the chapel of the workers' colony around the Güell textile mill he builds his model upside down: cords hung from a board, weighted with small shot bags in proportion to the loads each member must carry, photographed and then inverted to give the line the stone should follow. Gravity draws the plan; he only copies it. The crypt is finished and in use from 1915. The church that was to stand on top of it is never begun, the family having stopped the money in 1914.
stops.quote: The straight line belongs to Man. The curved line belongs to God.
stops.quote_source: Antoni Gaudí in conversation, c.1920-1926, recorded in Joan Bergós, Gaudí, l'home i l'obra (Barcelona: Aymà, 1954), p. 91; a similar formulation also appears in Pierre Albert-Birot, so some sources dispute the attribution
suggested_refs: The inverted funicular model for the Colònia Güell chapel, the laboratory for the Sagrada Família
sources: Colònia Güell archive; UNESCO nomination file

stops.name: Park Güell, sixty lots and two buyers
stops.date_confidence: attested; the work runs 1900-1914 and the land passes to the city as a public park
stops.campa: Güell buys a bare hill above the city called Muntanya Pelada and proposes a garden city of sixty houses on it for buyers who want air. Gaudí lays the roads along the contours, carries them on viaducts of unsquared stone leaning inward like a colonnade of trees, roofs the market hall on eighty-six Doric columns, and runs a bench around the terrace above in a serpentine sheathed with broken tile and shaped to the human back. Two lots sell. The land passes to the city, which opens it as a public park.
stops.quote: At that time Gaudi was little-known outside Spain, though nowadays universally recognized as one of the great pioneers of modern architecture, and his buildings, particularly the Cathedral of the Holy Family, and also the fantastic rambling park in the hilly suburbs of Barcelona, made a great impact on my imagination.
stops.quote_source: David Gascoyne, Journal 1936-1937 (Enitharmon Press, London, 1980), quoted in The Spanish Front: Writers on the Civil War, ed. Valentine Cunningham (1986)
suggested_refs: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, El arte de Gaudí (Ediciones Omega, Barcelona, 1950), which reads the park's ceramic serpents and spirals as a symbol grammar
sources: Park Güell development records; standard biographies

stops.name: Bellesguard, building on a king's ruin
stops.date_confidence: attested; built 1900-1909. Coordinates corrected here by roughly 370 m
stops.campa: On the slope below Tibidabo stand the remains of the house where Martí l'Humà, last king of the house of Barcelona, kept a court and died in 1410. Jaume Figueras's widow, María Sagués, owns the ground. Gaudí raises a narrow tower house of slate-coloured schist quarried on the spot, squared and vertical, the most Gothic thing he ever builds, and it goes up on the ground where the dynasty ended. The medieval walls he leaves where they are in the garden, as walls rather than as ruins to be admired.
suggested_refs: The surviving walls of Martí l'Humà's residence, incorporated into the Bellesguard grounds

stops.name: Casa Batlló, the house of bones
stops.date_confidence: attested for the commission and the remodelling, 1904-1906; the dragon reading of the roofline is popular tradition and rests on no statement of Gaudí's
stops.campa: The Batlló family owns a dull block on the Passeig de Gràcia and means to pull it down. Gaudí persuades them to keep it and reskins it instead. The lower floor grows columns like femurs, the first-floor window takes the outline of a jaw, and the city starts calling it the house of bones. The tiled roof arches over the street front in a scaled ridge Barcelona reads as a dragon's back with Saint George's cross planted in it. Within a few years, in Buenos Aires, Eduardo Rodríguez Ortega casts an iron dragon of his own onto Avenida Rivadavia, and the sources cannot agree which of Gaudí's dragons he was copying.
suggested_refs: The dragon gate of Avenida Rivadavia, Buenos Aires, an explicit quotation of Gaudí by Eduardo Rodríguez Ortega

stops.name: Palma de Mallorca, the choir screen removed
stops.date_confidence: attested; the work runs 1904-1914 and ends unfinished after disputes with the chapter and with Joan Rubió
stops.campa: Bishop Pere Campins wants his cathedral to work as a liturgy again and brings Gaudí over the water to do it. Gaudí takes out the baroque choir screen that has stood in the middle of the nave for centuries, moves the stalls into the presbytery, unwalls the Gothic windows, and hangs an enormous wrought-iron canopy over the altar. The chapter fights him, and in the end so does his own collaborator Joan Rubió. He leaves in 1914 with the scheme half done and no intention of finishing it.
suggested_refs: The cathedral chapter records of Palma on the Gaudí restoration and its abandonment
sources: Cathedral chapter records, Palma; standard biographies

segments.name: Passeig de Gràcia and the House on the Hill

stops.name: Park Güell, the show house nobody bought
stops.date_confidence: attested; the house is built 1903-1905 by Francesc Berenguer as a demonstration house and Gaudí buys it in 1906
stops.campa: Berenguer had built a demonstration house inside the failed development to show what living on the hill might be like, and nobody bought it. Gaudí buys it himself and moves in with his father Francesc, then close to ninety, and his orphaned niece Rosa Egea. He will live in this house for nineteen years and walk from it down to the Sagrada Família and back, the better part of an hour each way, on most of the days of his life. His father dies here in the same year they move in.
suggested_refs: The Gaudí House Museum in Park Güell, opened 28 September 1963 with his furniture and effects

stops.name: Passeig de Gràcia, the quarry begun
stops.date_confidence: attested; the project is presented to the city council on 2 February 1906 and construction runs 1906-1912
stops.campa: Pere Milà and his wife Roser Segimon present the plans for their new house to the city council. What rises is a building with no straight load-bearing wall anywhere in it, a stone skin hung on iron beams so that every partition inside can be moved by whoever lives there, its front cut in undulating courses of Garraf and Vilafranca limestone. Barcelona names it La Pedrera, the quarry, and does not mean it kindly. The council fines the owners for a building that breaks every dimension in the by-laws.
suggested_refs: The Barcelona city council file on Casa Milà, including the fines for exceeding the by-laws

stops.name: Montserrat, the first glorious mystery
stops.date_confidence: attested for the commission; the monument work and his devotional visits to the mountain run c.1900-1916
stops.campa: The Rosary path climbs the mountain behind the monastery and each mystery on it is given to a different architect and sculptor. Gaudí takes the first of the glorious mysteries, the Resurrection, and works it out with the sculptor Josep Llimona directly against the rock face, so that the monument and the cliff are one piece of geology. He had joined the Centre Excursionista de Catalunya at twenty-seven, in a society that walked this country as a way of holding it. He is up here often, on foot, among pilgrims.
suggested_refs: The First Glorious Mystery monument on the Rosary path at Montserrat, with Josep Llimona
sources: Rosary Monument commission records; standard biographies

stops.name: Casa Milà, the certificate and the last house
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Milà couple moved in after the council authorised occupancy in October 1911, and the certificate of completion is dated 31 October 1912
stops.campa: He signs the paper stating that the building has been completed according to his direction and is ready to be let. On the roof stand the chimneys and stair heads he has dressed in stone and broken marble, helmeted things facing in every direction over the Eixample. His niece Rosa Egea dies this same year at the Park Güell house, and the household that formed around him in 1876, when his mother died, is finished. It is the last private house he builds.
stops.quote: What I saw in Barcelona, Gaudí, was the work of such strength, such faith, of an extraordinary technical capacity, manifested during a whole life of genius; of a man who carved the stones before his eyes in well thought out pattern. Gaudí is the 'builder' of the turn of the century, a man adept with stone, iron and brick.
suggested_refs: Gaudí's certificate of completion for Casa Milà, 31 October 1912

stops.name: Barcelona, the year the commissions stop
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The economy turns, the private clients go, and Gaudí lets them go. From this year he takes nothing but the temple. He lives on what the almsgiving allows and goes out into the city on foot to ask shopkeepers and strangers for money for the building. Francesc Berenguer, who had built beside him for thirty years, died the year before. Josep Torras i Bages, Bishop of Vic and the closest thing he had to a confessor of the intellect, dies in 1916, and Eusebi Güell in 1918.
stops.quote: For the first time since I had been in Barcelona I went to have a look at the cathedral, a modern cathedral, and one of the most hideous buildings in the world.
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, Homage to Catalonia (Secker & Warburg, 1938)
suggested_refs: The alms round: Gaudí soliciting subscriptions in the streets of Barcelona for the temple

stops.name: Sagrada Família, the design for the Passion
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1917 design; none of the facade is built in his lifetime
stops.campa: He draws the Passion facade this year and will not live to build a stone of it. The drawing shows a portico carried on leaning bones of columns, gaunt where the Nativity front he has been raising is dense with birds and flowers and shepherds. The design is left for whoever comes after him, and the men who come after him will argue for a century over how much of the result is his. He tells the temple's board that people will be frightened by it and that it should be built anyway.
stops.quote: Sagrada Familia...is the greatest piece of creative architecture in the last twenty-five years. It is spirit symbolised in stone!
stops.quote_source: Louis Sullivan, quoted in Thomas E. Tallmadge, 'The Expiatory Temple of the Holy Family,' Western Architect XXXI (March 1922)
suggested_refs: Gaudí's 1917 drawing for the Passion facade, the basis of all later work on that front

stops.name: Sant Felip Neri, the daily mass
stops.date_confidence: attested for the daily habit in his final years; no source fixes when it began, so the date is an approximation
stops.campa: Every day he walks down from the temple into the Gothic quarter, to a small church on a square with a fountain in it, and hears mass and makes his confession. The walk is long and he is old and getting poorer. His clothes come apart on him and are mended with pins; people who pass him on the way take him for a beggar, and he carries nothing on him that gives his name. In 1902 the painter Joan Llimona used his face for a figure of Saint Philip Neri, the saint of this church.
suggested_refs: The church of Sant Felip Neri and its square, the daily destination of Gaudí's last years
sources: Contemporary accounts of collaborators, cited in standard biographies

stops.name: Barcelona, beaten for speaking Catalan
stops.date_confidence: attested for the incident at the Jocs Florals in 1920; the canonical Eixample pin is used because no source gives a precise location. One lens of this research tied the beating to Primo de Rivera, whose coup came three years later
stops.campa: At the Floral Games, the poetry contest that is also the yearly parade of the Catalan language, the police break up the celebration and Gaudí is beaten while insisting on speaking Catalan. He is sixty-eight years old. The language is the one political position he holds without any qualification, and he holds it in the plainest way available to him: by refusing to answer in another, whoever is asking and whatever they are carrying. Nothing comes of the assault and nobody is charged.
suggested_refs: The Jocs Florals of 1920 and the police action against the Catalan-language celebrations

stops.name: Sant Just i Sant Pastor, arrested for the dead of 1714
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the destination, the arrest and the fifty pesetas bail; the coordinate is an approximation of the Plaça de Sant Just, as no source in this research supplied one. A lens of this research placed the arrest at Sant Felip Neri after a Sant Josep Oriol procession, which no source supports
stops.campa: On the eleventh of September, the day Barcelona fell to Bourbon arms in 1714, he sets out for a mass said for the Catalans killed in that siege. Primo de Rivera has held power for a year and the commemoration is banned. The Guardia Civil stop him on his way to the basilica; he answers them in Catalan and they take him in. It is the second time in four years that the police have laid hands on him over the same refusal. He is seventy-two. He is released on fifty pesetas' bail and goes back to the site.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of Sants Just i Pastor and the banned 1924 commemoration of the Catalan dead of 1714
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoni_Gaudí (arrest of 11 September 1924, released on 50 pesetas bail)

stops.name: Sagrada Família, the room beside the workshop
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move in late 1925; the exact date is not given by the sources
stops.campa: He sells the house in Park Güell and moves into a small room next to the model workshop on the site, among the plaster casts and the hanging cords, and does not leave it again. He is seventy-three and lives under something like a rule: mass, the drawing board, the scaffold, the alms round. Visitors find him gaunt, his suit held together with safety pins, and find that he will talk about nothing at all except the building going up around him. He has been on this site for forty-two years.
stops.quote: Men may be divided into two types: men of words and men of action. The first speaks; the latter act. I am of the second group. I lack the means to express myself adequately. I would not be able to explain to anyone my artistic concepts. I have not yet concretised them. I never had time to reflect on them. My hours have been spent in my work.
stops.quote_source: Antoni Gaudí, interview in La Razón, 1913, cited in Gijs van Hensbergen, Gaudí (HarperCollins), introduction p. xxxii
suggested_refs: The model workshop of the Sagrada Família, destroyed in 1936, and Gaudí's room beside it
sources: Contemporary accounts of visitors and collaborators, cited in standard biographies

stops.name: Gran Via de les Corts Catalanes, tram number thirty
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the tram; the pin is the stretch of the Gran Via between Carrer de Girona and Carrer de Bailèn named by the sources, after two lenses of this research placed the accident a kilometre away in different directions
stops.campa: Walking from the temple toward Sant Felip Neri for evening prayer he crosses the Gran Via and is knocked down by tram number thirty. The crossing is between Carrer de Girona and Carrer de Bailèn, ten minutes on foot from his own building site. He has no papers on him and his clothes are worn through. Taxi drivers refuse to carry him, and one of them is fined for it afterwards. A civil guard eventually gets him into a cart, and he is taken to the pauper's ward of the old general hospital, unidentified: one more old man run over in the street.
suggested_refs: Contemporary Barcelona press reports of the tram accident of 7 June 1926

stops.name: Hospital de la Santa Creu, three days
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinates corrected here after three separate values in this research pool, none of which matched the building
stops.campa: He lies in the ward for the indigent until the following day, when the chaplain of the Sagrada Família recognises him. The care given him in the first hours was rudimentary, of the kind a ward for the destitute affords, and by then the injuries are past treating. Friends arrive and want him moved to a private clinic and he refuses, saying that he belongs among the poor. He dies on the tenth of June, three days after the accident, at seventy-three. The hospital building now holds the national library of Catalonia.
suggested_refs: The old Hospital de la Santa Creu, Carrer de l'Hospital 56, now the Biblioteca de Catalunya
sources: Hospital records and contemporary press accounts, June 1926

stops.name: Barcelona, the funeral crosses the city
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pin is an approximate midpoint of the route, which no source maps in detail
stops.campa: The papal nuncio grants the dispensation to bury him inside the temple. Barcelona had spent much of his last decade calling that temple an embarrassment and had never buried an architect on this scale before. The cortege leaves the hospital in the old town and goes up through the Eixample to the Sagrada Família, and the streets on the route are full the whole way: workers, clergy, the city government, people who had watched him go past for years with a collecting box in his hand.
suggested_refs: Contemporary Barcelona press accounts of the funeral procession of 12 June 1926

stops.name: Crypt of the Sagrada Família, the chapel of Carmen
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is laid in the crypt beneath the chapel of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, in the one part of the building he did not design, Villar's foundations being what he had inherited in 1883. Decades of critical contempt follow. Salvador Dalí leads the reassessment of the 1950s, with a retrospective at the Saló del Tinell in 1956 and New York the year after; Juan Eduardo Cirlot, who reads the ceramic serpents and spirals of Park Güell as a grammar of symbols, had published El arte de Gaudí in 1950. A cause for his canonisation opens in Barcelona, and in 2025 he is declared Venerable.
suggested_refs: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, El arte de Gaudí (Ediciones Omega, Barcelona, 1950)
The 1956 Saló del Tinell retrospective and the 1957 Museum of Modern Art exhibition
sources: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoni_Gaudí (the Dalí-led reassessment; the canonization cause, whose chronology es- and en-wikipedia date differently, 1998/2000 against 2003)

stops.name: Sagrada Família, the tower of Jesus Christ
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A hundred years after his death the central tower reaches structural completion at a hundred and seventy-two and a half metres, and the church becomes the tallest in the world. It has been paid for from the first stone by alms and tickets, some twenty-five million euros a year, and the interior work is projected to run to 2028. On the tenth of June, the centenary of the day he died in the pauper's ward, the tower is blessed and inaugurated by Pope Leo XIV.
stops.quote: After lunch, in sudden rain, we go to see Gaudí's masterpiece, the still unfinished church of the Sagrada Familia or Holy Family. There is nothing in the world like it. It is Disney whimsicality raised to the level of soaring nobility.
stops.quote_source: Anthony Burgess, Homage to QWERT YUIOP: Essays (Hutchinson, London, 1986), p. 71
suggested_refs: The Tower of Jesus Christ, structurally complete 20 February 2026 at 172.5 m
